passage:
Day 1. Lalremsiami stroked her toddler's back to settle him at bedtime, but he squirmed and pushed her hand away. She stopped, puzzled, and just sat beside him for a while, unsure what she had done wrong.

Day 4. Her mother-in-law, Shalini, was ill and restless. Lalremsiami held her hand and stroked it slowly. Shalini's breathing eased and her fingers curled around hers.

Day 7. At bedtime Lalremsiami had learned to check first, so she asked her son, "Back rub or just sit?" He said, "Sit," so she did, keeping her hands in her lap. After a few minutes he leaned against her shoulder and yawned.

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami do to Shalini's hand on day 4?
qa.a: She held it and stroked it slowly.

qa.q: What did the toddler's squirming and pushing away suggest, and what else could it mean?
qa.a: It suggested the touch did not feel comforting to him that night, though he might simply have been too restless or ticklish. Lalremsiami took it as his choice.

qa.q: What small change helped at bedtime on day 7?
qa.a: Lalremsiami asked whether he wanted a back rub or just company, and followed his choice.

qa.q: How might Shalini have felt when her hand was stroked?
qa.a: Shalini seemed comforted, since her breathing eased and her fingers curled around Lalremsiami's hand.

grounding: Illustrates soothing touch that helps only when the receiver's comfort, seen in breath or flinching, shows it is welcome.

passage: Bidisha, I will tell you what my grandmother's hands taught me. Elder here, Lakshmi. When my own daughter was small and feverish, I stroked her back in slow circles and watched her face. If her breath softened and her shoulders dropped, I kept going. Once she flinched and pulled forward, so I stopped and asked her what she wanted, and she wanted a cool cloth instead. With my old aunt in the hospital, I held her hand and she squeezed back. Care is not what the giver intends; it is what the other person can take in. So watch the breath, watch the body. If they pull away, that is an answer.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi hold in the hospital?
qa.a: Lakshmi held the old aunt's hand.

qa.q: What did the flinch by Lakshmi's daughter suggest, and how did Lakshmi respond?
qa.a: It suggested the back stroking was not comforting at that moment, so Lakshmi stopped and asked. The flinch could also be discomfort from the fever, but asking found what she wanted.

qa.q: What can a caregiver look for to know whether touch is helping?
qa.a: A caregiver can watch for a softening breath and dropped shoulders, and stop if the person pulls away or flinches.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi's daughter have felt when Lakshmi stopped and asked?
qa.a: She probably felt listened to and in control, since her wish for a cool cloth was followed.

grounding: Elder's account of soothing touch whose helpfulness is judged by the receiver's relaxing breath or flinching.

passage: The storm knocked the power out at nine, and Tarun was alone with his nephew Yash for the night while his sister was on hospital duty. Four-year-old Yash woke screaming at the first crack of thunder. In the dark, Tarun sat on the bed and began stroking his back in slow circles, the way his own mother used to. Yash stiffened and wriggled away, crying harder. Tarun paused, stung for a second, then made himself watch instead of pushing on. By the phone torch he saw Yash reaching out, fingers spread. He took the small hand and held it still, no stroking. Yash's breathing slowed. His shoulders dropped. After a while he tugged Tarun's hand onto his head. "There," he mumbled. Tarun kept his palm resting there, not moving, until the rain softened and Yash's breath went long and even.

qa.q: Where was Tarun's sister that night?
qa.a: On hospital duty.

qa.q: How did Tarun feel when Yash wriggled away from the back-stroking?
qa.a: Tarun felt a moment's sting of rejection, then chose to watch Yash's cues calmly instead of pushing on.

qa.q: What helped Yash settle, and how did Tarun know?
qa.a: Holding his hand still and later resting a palm on his head; Tarun could tell because Yash's breathing slowed and his shoulders dropped.

qa.q: What might the stroking have felt like for Yash in the storm?
qa.a: Frightened by the thunder, Yash may have felt the stroking as too much, so he stiffened; a still hand felt safer to him.

grounding: Shows a carer soothing a child and letting the child's breathing and flinching, not the carer's intention, decide which touch helps.

passage: Every evening after work, Chaitanya took the lift up to the seventh floor of the Jayanagar flat to sit with Dada, whose name, Harish, was still painted on the brass plate beside the door. Since the stroke his speech came slowly, and he spent afternoons by the window. Tonight he was restless, plucking at the blanket. Chaitanya sat down and began stroking the back of his hand with a thumb. His fingers stopped plucking; his breath came out long, and his eyes half closed. Encouraged, Chaitanya moved to rub his upper arm too. Dada flinched and pulled the arm in. Chaitanya stopped at once. "Sorry, Dada. Hand only?" He gave a slow nod and turned his palm up. Chaitanya went back to the hand, watching his face, and stayed until he fell asleep.

qa.q: Which floor was Dada's flat on?
qa.a: The seventh floor.

qa.q: What was Dada likely feeling when Chaitanya stroked the back of his hand?
qa.a: He seemed calmer and comforted, since his plucking stopped and his breath came out long, though he might also simply have been tired.

qa.q: What did Chaitanya do well when Dada flinched?
qa.a: Chaitanya stopped at once, apologised, asked 'Hand only?' and followed the answer, letting Dada's comfort decide the touch.

qa.q: What would have changed if Chaitanya had kept rubbing Dada's arm after the flinch?
qa.a: The touch meant as comfort would have become unwelcome, and Dada might have grown more restless instead of falling asleep.

grounding: Shows a young adult soothing an elder's hand and reading relaxed breath and a flinch to decide which touch helps.

passage:
"Nani, can't sleep again?"
Jahnavi Nani shook her head against the pillow. "The clock is too loud."
Ishita sat on the edge of the bed and began rubbing slow circles on her back. "Better?"
Nani went rigid. "Beta, not the back. It feels like ants."
"Oh! Sorry." Ishita pulled her hand away. "What would feel nice?"
"Just the hand. Like your Nana used to."
Ishita took Nani's thin hand and stroked the back of it with her thumb. "Like this?"
"Mm. Slower."
"Like this?"
"Yes." Nani let out a long breath. Her shoulders sank into the mattress. "You have his hands."
"You always say that."
"Because it's true." Her eyes closed. "Stay till I sleep?"
"I'm not going anywhere."
Ishita kept stroking, watching her breathing slow, until the clock didn't matter any more.

qa.q: What did Nani say about the clock?
qa.a: The clock is too loud.

qa.q: How did Jahnavi Nani feel when Ishita rubbed her back?
qa.a: She felt uncomfortable, going rigid and saying it felt like ants, even though Ishita meant it to soothe.

qa.q: How did Ishita find the right way to comfort Nani?
qa.a: She stopped at once, asked what would feel nice, and adjusted the speed until Nani's breathing slowed and her shoulders sank.

qa.q: What would have changed if Ishita had kept rubbing Nani's back?
qa.a: Nani would have stayed rigid and awake, uncomfortable despite the kind intention, and might not have felt able to say so again.

grounding: Shows a young carer soothing an elder and letting the elder's comfort, not her own intention, decide the touch.

passage:
The first night I stayed with Nani after her fall, I thought I knew how to comfort her. My cousin Akash had told me, "Rub her back, she loves that." So when she couldn't sleep, I started stroking between her shoulder blades.
Her whole body went stiff. Her breath caught. "Not there, Tejas," she whispered, and I stopped at once.
Later I understood that her back was still bruised from the fall; what used to soothe her now hurt.
So I tried her hand instead, slow strokes with my thumb along the back of it. This time her breathing grew longer and her fingers curled around mine. Within ten minutes she was asleep.
Looking back, what I took from that night was simple: her body tells me what helps, not my good intentions, and not what worked for her last year.

qa.q: What had Akash told Tejas to do?
qa.a: Akash had said, "Rub her back, she loves that."

qa.q: What did Nani's stiff body and caught breath suggest?
qa.a: They suggested Nani was in pain and uncomfortable with the back rub rather than soothed; Tejas later understood her back was still bruised from the fall.

qa.q: What did Tejas do differently, and why did it work?
qa.a: Tejas switched to slow thumb strokes on the back of her hand and watched her breathing lengthen, letting her response guide the touch.

qa.q: How might Nani have felt if Tejas had kept rubbing her back?
qa.a: She would likely have felt more pain and less able to rest, and perhaps unheard, since her stiffening was already saying stop.

grounding: When stroking an elder to soothe her, the carer watches her breath and flinching, because her comfort, not the carer's intention, decides whether the touch helps.
